Solid State Physics · Properties of Solids

Module I — Crystal structure & X-rays

Theory notes: concepts, results and what every symbol means

Crystal, lattice, basis

in one lineA crystal is one group of atoms (the basis) stamped onto every point of an endless regular grid (the lattice).

Crystalline vs amorphous

Solids come in two kinds, and the difference is just how far the tidiness reaches.

  • Crystalline — the atomic pattern repeats predictably over enormous distances. This is long-range order: knowing where one atom sits lets you predict one a million atoms away. Diamond, quartz, salt, copper.
    • Single crystal — the pattern runs unbroken through the whole piece.
    • Polycrystalline — many small tidy grains pointing in random directions, meeting at grain boundaries. Most metals you handle are like this.
  • Amorphous — tidy over only a few atoms (short-range order), then it loses the plot. Glass, plastics. It happens when a liquid is cooled so fast the atoms freeze before they can line up.

Crystals form because the ordered arrangement has the lowest energy. Nature takes it whenever it is given time.

Lattice, basis, structure — keep these three apart

These three words get mixed up constantly, and separating them earns marks on its own.

  • Lattice — an imaginary set of points, repeating forever. No atoms in it at all. Its defining property: every point has exactly the same view of its surroundings as every other point.
  • Basis — the actual atom, or group of atoms, that you put at each point.
  • Structure — what you get when you do that:
wherethe endless regular array of points, all with identical surroundings (no atoms yet)the atom, or group of atoms, attached to every lattice pointthe finished pattern of atoms in space

Think of patterned wallpaper. The lattice is the set of positions where the motif gets stamped; the basis is the motif; the wallpaper is the structure. Two very different wallpapers can use the same stamping positions.

You travel between lattice points using a translation vector — a recipe of whole-number steps along three chosen directions :

wherelattice translation vector: it carries you from one lattice point to anotherprimitive vectors, the three edges of the primitive cellwhole numbers (positive, negative or zero); each choice reaches one lattice point

If whole numbers alone can reach every point, those vectors are called primitive.

Unit cells, and counting the atoms inside one

A unit cell is the small box you repeat to build the whole crystal.

  • Primitive cell — the smallest box possible. It works out to exactly one lattice point per cell, with volume .
  • Conventional cell — usually a bigger, nicer box (a cube, say) with extra points at the body centre or face centres. It holds more than one point, but we use it because it shows the symmetry, which a skewed primitive cell hides.

An atom on a corner or a face is shared with neighbouring boxes, so you only count your share. A corner is shared by 8 boxes, a face by 2, an atom fully inside belongs to you alone:

whereeffective number of atoms (lattice points) belonging to one cellatoms wholly inside the cell: each counts 1atoms on the faces: each is shared by 2 cells, so counts atoms at the corners: each is shared by 8 cells, so counts
learn this by heart

Simple cubic  ·  Body-centred cubic (BCC)  ·  Face-centred cubic (FCC)

One more cell is worth a sentence. The Wigner–Seitz cell: stand on a lattice point, draw a line to each neighbour, and cut every line in half with a perpendicular wall. The region you are left standing in is the cell — primitive and fully symmetric. Remember that recipe: the identical construction done in reciprocal space later gives the Brillouin zone.

Drawing a Wigner–Seitz cell — do it once by hand

Draw it yourself in 2-D once and you own it for good, because the 3-D cell and every Brillouin zone later is the same four moves: join, halve, bisect, keep the middle. Step through the construction, then switch the lattice underneath and watch the same four moves give a different shape.

where marks get lost

Two ways this goes wrong in an exam. Bisecting the wrong thing: the bisector is perpendicular to the line joining the two points and passes through its midpoint — not perpendicular to a cell edge. Stopping too early or too late: include a neighbour and its bisector may simply sit outside and do nothing (harmless), but leave out a near one and the cell comes out too big. Safe habit: bisect every neighbour out to about the nearest distance, then keep the innermost region.

Symmetry & the 5-fold ban

in one lineA crystal can only have 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6-fold rotation symmetry — anything else cannot fill space without leaving gaps.

The four symmetry operations

A symmetry operation is any move that leaves the crystal looking exactly as it did. There are four kinds:

  1. Translation — slide by .
  2. Rotation — turn by about an axis. We call it an -fold axis: means a quarter turn restores it.
  3. Reflection () — mirror it through a plane.
  4. Inversion () — push every point through a centre to the opposite side, .

Collect the operations that leave one point fixed (everything except translation) and you have a point group. Add translations too and you get a space group.

learn this by heart

2-D: 10 point groups, 17 space groups.   3-D: 32 point groups, 230 space groups. Four cheap marks.

Why 5-fold symmetry is impossible

You can tile a floor with triangles, squares or hexagons and leave no gaps — but never with regular pentagons. Crystals face the same restriction, and there is a short proof.

Bravais lattices

in one lineOnce only the legal symmetries are allowed, exactly 7 box shapes and 14 distinct lattices survive in 3-D. This is a table to memorise.

The table

A box is described by three edge lengths and the three angles between them . Sorting boxes by symmetry gives 7 crystal systems. Allowing extra points at the body centre (), all face centres () or one pair of faces () gives 14 Bravais lattices.

In 2-D the answer is 4 systems, 5 lattices — oblique, rectangular primitive, rectangular centred, square, hexagonal. The rectangular system is the one that supports two.

All 14, in the round

The table is only half the memory. What actually sticks is the shape: which box got squashed, which got sheared, and where the extra points sit. Walk the whole list below — pick a system, then a centring — and say the row of the table out loud as each cell appears.

Two things to take from the spin. First, a corner point is shared by 8 cells and a face point by 2, so owns point, owns , owns and owns — the counts printed on each cell. Second, the seven systems are one chain of lowering symmetry: start from the cube and stretch, then unequalise, then shear, and you arrive at triclinic, which keeps nothing but the repetition itself.

where marks get lost

“Why is there no face-centred tetragonal lattice?” is a favourite. Answer: because it is not new — a face-centred tetragonal cell can be redrawn as a smaller body-centred tetragonal cell (rotate the axes and shrink by ). A centring only counts as a separate Bravais lattice if it cannot be re-described as an existing one. That test is what trims the list to 14.

Directions & Miller indices

in one lineDirections get square brackets . Planes get round brackets and are labelled by the reciprocals of where they cut the axes.

Naming a direction: [uvw]

Draw the arrow from the origin, read its components in units of , and scale to the smallest whole numbers. Square brackets.

  • — one specific direction. A minus sign is written as a bar on top: is the direction.
  • — the whole family that symmetry makes equivalent. In a cube, means all six cube-edge directions.

In a cubic crystal the angle between two directions is just the ordinary angle between two vectors:

whereangle between the two planes (the angle between their normals)Miller indices of the first and second plane (cubic crystal)

Naming a plane: Miller indices (hkl)

Four steps, every single time:

  1. Find where the plane cuts the three axes, measured in units of . Call them .
  2. Take the reciprocals: .
  3. Multiply through to clear fractions, giving smallest whole numbers.
  4. Write them in round brackets, no commas: .

A plane parallel to an axis never cuts it, so that intercept is — and . That is the whole reason for step 2: reciprocals turn an unusable infinity into a perfectly good zero.

Worked example. Intercepts → → reciprocals → multiply by 2 → .

Brackets matter: is one set of parallel planes; is the symmetry-equivalent family.

Drawing — the same recipe, run backwards

The question comes the other way round just as often: “sketch the plane in a cubic cell”. Naming runs intercepts → reciprocals; drawing runs reciprocals → intercepts, then you join them. Four moves: invert, mark, join, shade.

Three habits that keep the marks:

  • Mark the origin first. A plane that passes through the origin has an intercept of , and is not an index — shift the origin one cell along, or draw the next parallel plane of the same family instead. They have the same name.
  • A zero index means “never cuts”. Do not look for an intercept: run the plane parallel to that axis, right through the cell.
  • A bar means the negative side. Step into the cell behind the origin rather than trying to squeeze the plane into the first one.
learn this by heart

In a cubic crystal, the direction is perpendicular to the plane . This one fact turns most plane questions into simple vector arithmetic.

And a direction lies inside the plane exactly when whereMiller indices of the planeindices of the directionthe test: if it is zero the direction lies in the plane, or parallel to it (because "lies in the plane" means "perpendicular to the plane's normal"). No drawing required.

Packing & structures

in one lineTreat atoms as hard spheres. Where they touch fixes in terms of — and that gives you the coordination number and the fraction of space filled.

The two numbers that describe a packing

  • Coordination number () — how many nearest neighbours actually touch a given atom.
  • Packing fraction () — what fraction of the box is really filled with sphere: wherepacking fraction: the share of the cell volume filled by atomsatomic radius (atoms treated as touching hard spheres)volume of one atomvolume of the cubic cell

Everything follows from one question: along which line do the spheres touch? Answer that and you have in terms of ; the rest is arithmetic.

Close packing and the c/a ratio

FCC and HCP are both the tightest possible stacking of equal spheres — both give and . They differ only in the stacking order of the close-packed layers: HCP repeats , FCC repeats .

Diamond & NaCl

in one lineAll three are an FCC lattice with a two-atom basis — only the basis changes.

Diamond and zinc blende

  • Diamond — FCC lattice; basis = two identical atoms at and . So atoms per cube. Each atom has just 4 neighbours arranged tetrahedrally, at distance . Packing fraction only . Materials: C, Si, Ge, grey tin.
  • Zinc blende (ZnS) — identical geometry, but the two basis atoms are different elements. Coordination , 4 formula units per cube.
where marks get lost

“Why does diamond fill only 34% of space when FCC fills 74%?” Because its bonding is directional. Covalent bonds insist on the tetrahedral arrangement, and tetrahedra cannot pack tightly. Close packing () is what you get when bonding has no preferred direction, as in metals. Structure follows bonding.

Rock salt (NaCl)

  • FCC lattice; basis = one at and one at — displaced along a cube edge, not the diagonal.
  • 4 + 4 per cube (4 formula units). Coordination , octahedral.
  • The ions touch along the edge, so — the line you need for every NaCl numerical.

X-rays & reciprocal space

in one lineX-rays reflect off crystal planes only at special angles (). Describing that in “reciprocal space” turns the condition into a clean geometric picture.

Bragg's law

To resolve something of size you need a wave of comparable wavelength. Atomic spacings are about Å, which is the X-ray range — that is the entire reason crystallography uses X-rays and not visible light.

Picture the planes , spaced apart, as a stack of half-silvered mirrors. A ray reflecting off the second plane travels further than one off the first. Geometry makes that extra distance , and you get a bright reflection only when it equals a whole number of wavelengths:

learn this by heart
wherespacing between the reflecting planesglancing angle: between the X-ray beam and the planes (not to the normal)order of the reflection: 1, 2, 3, ...wavelength of the X-rays

is measured from the plane, not from the normal — that is the classic slip. is the order of the reflection.

Because , an -th order reflection from can always be relabelled a first-order reflection from — which is why tables list and reflections.

Laue's version — and why it is the same law

Laue looked atom by atom instead of plane by plane. For two scatterers separated by , with the incoming and outgoing directions, the extra path is . Demanding a whole number of wavelengths along each crystal axis gives Laue's three equations:

whereprimitive vectors of the lattice: difference of the unit vectors along the incident and scattered beamswhole numbers; they turn out to be the Miller indices of the reflecting planesorder of the reflectionX-ray wavelength

Rewriting these with direction cosines and turns them into , i.e. . Bragg and Laue are the same physics in different clothing — a standard short-answer question.

One refinement worth a line: real atoms are fuzzy clouds of electrons, not points. Waves scattered from different parts of the same cloud partly cancel, and cancel more as the angle grows. This is the atomic scattering factor, and it is why high-angle reflections come out systematically weaker.

The three X-ray diffraction methods

Bragg's law (first order, every plane real or imagined) has three quantities. An experiment fixes one or two and lets the crystal pick the rest. Since , we need ; with Å that means Å.

Lauesingle crystal, held stillwhite (0.2–2 Å) fixed, variescrystal symmetry, orienting crystals, strain (streaks = asterism)
Rotating crystalsingle crystal on a spindlemonochromatic fixed, variescell dimensions: spacing of the layer lines gives (then , )
Powder (Debye–Scherrer)fine powder, ~ crystallites/monochromatic fixed; and both varythe standard structure method; no single crystal needed

Laue: a flat-plate camera with films for transmitted and back-reflected spots. Each set of planes picks out the wavelength that satisfies Bragg's law, so you get spots; a crystal with a 4-fold axis along the beam gives a 4-fold pattern. It cannot give the full structure, because several wavelengths and orders can land on one spot.

Rotating crystal: one axis (say ) along the rotation axis, film on a cylinder round it. Planes give the central layer line, the line above, and so on; the layer-line spacing measures the repeat distance along the axis.

Powder: for each the reflected rays from all the randomly oriented crystallites lie on a cone of semi-vertical angle ; the cones cut the film strip in arcs. Measure the arc spacing on a camera of radius : , then from Bragg's law.

The reciprocal lattice

Here is the idea in plain terms. A family of parallel planes is fully described by two things: which way it faces, and how far apart the planes are. So represent the whole family by a single arrow — pointing along the plane normal, with length inversely proportional to the spacing:

wherereciprocal lattice vector belonging to the planes spacing of those planesunit vector perpendicular to the planes

Collect the arrows for every possible family and their tips form a new lattice — the reciprocal lattice. It lives in "-space", where distances have units of 1/length, not in ordinary space. Closely-spaced planes → long arrow → point far from the origin.

Its building vectors come from the real ones:

whereprimitive vectors of the reciprocal latticeprimitive vectors of the real latticevolume of the real primitive cellvector (cross) product; "cyclically" means uses and uses

built so that while . The reciprocal cell has volume .

learn this by heart

Reciprocals of the cubic lattices — a near-guaranteed question:

  • simple cubic → simple cubic (spacing )
  • BCC → FCC
  • FCC → BCC

Properties of the reciprocal lattice

  1. Each reciprocal lattice point stands for one set of parallel planes of the direct lattice.
  2. Its distance from the origin is inversely proportional to the spacing of those planes ().
  3. The volume of the reciprocal unit cell is inversely proportional to that of the direct cell ().
  4. The reciprocal unit cell need not be a parallelepiped: one usually takes its Wigner–Seitz cell, the Brillouin zone.
  5. The direct lattice is the reciprocal of its own reciprocal. SC is self-reciprocal; BCC and FCC are reciprocal to each other.

Brillouin zones

Now combine the two ideas. Diffraction happens when the wave's change of direction matches a reciprocal lattice arrow, . The scattering is elastic so ; squaring gives

wherewave vector of the incident wave, a reciprocal lattice vectorits length ends on the plane that bisects at right angles: that is the Bragg condition

Read geometrically that says: a wave diffracts exactly when the tip of lands on the perpendicular bisector plane of a reciprocal lattice vector.

Those bisector planes act as walls. The region around the origin enclosed by the nearest walls is the first Brillouin zone — which is simply the Wigner–Seitz cell from earlier, built in reciprocal space instead of real space.
